did_you_know.text: Did you know? At the dedication of the Temple, Solomon assembled the elders of Israel, the heads of the tribes, and the leaders of the ancestral families to bring up the Ark of the Lord’s Covenant from the City of David, which is Zion.
Did you know? The Ark was brought up during the month of Ethanim, the festival month—that is, the seventh month, during the Feast of Tabernacles.
Did you know? According to the text, the Ark contained only the two stone tablets that Moses had placed there at Horeb—the tablets on which the Lord made the covenant with Israel.

Did you know? When the priests came out of the sanctuary, a cloud filled the Temple of the Lord, so that the priests could not stand and minister. The text explains that the cloud represented the Temple being filled with the glory of the Lord.
Did you know? Solomon describes the Temple as a “noble house”—a magnificent building dedicated to the Lord’s name, but not a place that limits God’s presence.
Did you know? In his prayer, Solomon emphasizes that even the heavens and the highest heavens cannot contain the Lord—much less the Temple he has built.
Did you know? Solomon’s prayer also includes the foreigner: he asks that the Lord hear the prayer of anyone who comes from a distant land for the sake of His name.
Did you know? Solomon acknowledges that there is no one who does not sin. Therefore, he describes the possibility of sin, defeat, and exile, along with repentance, supplication, and forgiveness.

Did you know? Solomon consecrated the inner court in front of the Temple as a place for offering sacrifices because the bronze altar was too small to hold all the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and fellowship offerings.
Did you know? The celebration of the Temple’s dedication lasted fourteen days: seven days for the festival and seven additional days. Afterward, the people returned home joyful and glad of heart.
